newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro MPs urged to follow voters on gene-food.
newsitem.headline: Euro MPs urged to follow voters on gene-food.

text.p: The European Parliament should take heed of a new survey showing that a majority of voters questioned oppose the development of genetically-modified food, environmental group Greenpeace said on Thursday.
The parliament is due to vote next Wednesday on a draft regulation, COM(93)631, on so-called "novel foods," which use new technology or are being sold for the first time in Europe.

The survey, conducted by Market & Opinion Research International (MORI), showed that 59 percent of Danes, Dutch, French, British, Italians and Swedes questioned were against genetically engineered food.
"The survey shows a clear majority of voters don't want it," Greenpeace campaigner Benny Haerlin told a news conference.
But he said that after six years of discussions Euro MPs were exhausted and likely to agree the new rules.
The survey showed that resistance was strongest in Sweden, where 76 percent of those surveyed were against, and lowest in Italy, where 44 percent were opposed.
In Britain, regarded by Greenpeace as being one of the countries most supportive of biotechnology, 51 percent were opposed.
A separate German survey by market research Institut GfK found that 74 percent of those covered wanted to stop gene-food.
Genetic engineering allows beer to ferment faster, cheese to mature quicker, pigs to grow larger, tomatoes to age more slowly and cereals to resist pests.

Greenpeace criticised the new rules -- a compromise struck in a parliament-Council of Ministers conciliation committee on November 28 -- saying that most genetically engineered foods would not be labelled.
Haerlin said that Euro MPs, who have little say over many EU decisions, had been corrupted by the extra power they had been given under the Maastricht Treaty and lost sight of voters' views.
The novel foods regulation is being adopted under new co-decision procedures giving the parliament the right to veto legislation.
"People who don't want to eat gene-food must have the right to know what is in their food," Haerlin said.

Only so-called "live" genetically modified food products -- containing organisms that could grow given soil and water -- and which were substantially different from conventional food, would have to be labelled.
Only about 20 percent of genetically engineered soybean products would have to be labelled, Haerlin estimated.
He said there were too many loopholes in the new rules, which would come into force by May.
For instance, it would be left to the European Commission to identify novel foods, decide whether they endangered consumers and whether labels were misleading.
Haerlin said the survey, in which 4,840 people were interviewed between December 11-20, was limited to six countries because of cost and a tight deadline.
